title: Kierkegaard
summary: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish thinker often called the father of existentialism. He was interested not in abstract systems but in the living, single individual who must make a choice and become themselves. He wrote about anxiety, despair and faith as the central events of inner life.
onEmotions: For Kierkegaard, heavy feelings are not obstacles but signposts: anxiety shows that you are free, despair that you have not yet fully become yourself. He believed they can't simply be removed — they have to be passed through, accepted as part of the self's becoming. He described three “stages of existence”: the aesthetic (life for the sake of impressions), the ethical (a life of choice and responsibility) and the religious (a personal relationship to the infinite). Each stage colors experience in its own way, and the transition between them often happens through a crisis — through a “leap,” a decision that can't be calculated in advance.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a tormenting feeling, but Kierkegaard saw something remarkable in it. In The Concept of Anxiety (the Danish word Angest is translated both as “dread” and as “anxiety”), he wrote that anxiety arises in the face of possibility. When a person looks into an open future where they could choose either this or that, their head spins, like someone looking down from a great height. Hence his famous image: anxiety is “the dizziness of freedom.” From this angle, anxiety isn't a sign that you're weak but a sign that you're free and your life isn't predetermined. Kierkegaard even believed that whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the most important thing. Anxiety is a school: through it we learn that our life is in our own hands.
anxiety.practice: Write down which possibility is making your “head spin” right now. What does this anxiety say about what is open to you?

quote.text: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

fear.text: Fear is a natural reaction to a threat, and there's nothing shameful in it. Kierkegaard drew an important distinction: fear in the narrow sense is always directed at something definite — an event, a person, a danger. Anxiety, by contrast, is directed at “nothing,” at an indefinite possibility. From this angle, you might say fear has an advantage: it has an object, it can be named. Sometimes it helps to ask yourself what exactly you're afraid of — and often behind a concrete fear lies a deeper anxiety about yourself and your choice. In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard wrote of faith as the resolve to act without guarantees. Following him, you could say: courage isn't the absence of fear, but taking a step together with it.
fear.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm afraid that…” — and then: “And behind this, perhaps, is an anxiety that I…”.

sadness.text: Sadness is familiar to many deep people, and Kierkegaard was one of them: all his life he wrote about his “melancholy” (in Danish, Tungsind — literally “heaviness of mind”). He didn't consider it simply a bad mood. In the second volume of Either/Or, his character Judge William says that melancholy is a sign that the spirit wants to break through: a person must “choose himself” rather than dissolve into diversions. From this angle, sadness may be not a malfunction but a question life is asking you personally: are you living the way you really want to? Kierkegaard didn't rush the answer. What matters is not to run from this question into busyness but to let it be heard — sadness has a right to its time.
sadness.practice: Ask your sadness: “What in my life do you want to remind me of?” Write down the answer without editing.

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest experiences, and no one has the right to hurry it. Kierkegaard himself lost his mother and several brothers and sisters early on, and then his father, and his thought is steeped in this experience. In Works of Love there's a reflection on love for the dead as the most unselfish and faithful form of love: the one who is gone can give nothing back, and so remembering them is a pure gift. From this angle, grief is love that continues when there's nowhere left to direct it. Kierkegaard called recollecting the dead one of the “works of love.” And there's a support to be found in this: your pain isn't only a loss but also faithfulness. To live through it is to go on loving.
grief.practice: Do one small “work of remembrance” today: write down a story, say a name, keep an object. How does your faithfulness feel?

loneliness.text: Loneliness is hard, and the wish to be rid of it is understandable. Kierkegaard, however, gave enormous importance to the idea of “the single individual” (den Enkelte) — the separate person who faces life on their own rather than dissolving into the “crowd” or the “public.” He criticized the crowd for relieving people of responsibility and making them faceless. From this angle, you might say that loneliness holds not only pain but also a place where you meet yourself. This doesn't mean you should live without people: in Works of Love, Kierkegaard insisted on love of the neighbor. But real closeness, in his view, is possible between those who remain themselves rather than dissolving into others. Loneliness can be the beginning of such closeness.
loneliness.practice: Write down one thing you think or feel on your own, not because it's what people around you do. How does it feel to be with this voice of your own?

quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
quote.source: “That Single Individual,” appendix to The Point of View for My Work as an Author (publ. 1859)

anger.text: Anger is an energy that speaks of a value that's been hurt, and there's nothing shameful in it. Kierkegaard wrote little about anger directly, but his ideas help us see it differently. In his treatise on despair (1849), he described various forms of a person's wrong relationship to themselves. One of them is “defiance” — the despairing wish to be yourself in spite of everything, a rebellion against a life that isn't the way we need it to be. From this angle, you might say that behind strong anger there is sometimes exactly this: pain that the world doesn't obey our idea of ourselves. Kierkegaard saw in such rebellion a strength of spirit, not a vice. The only question is where to direct it: against life, or toward becoming more honestly yourself.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: am I angry at a specific act, or at the fact that life doesn't match my idea of it? Write down what you notice.

shame.text: Shame is the feeling that you're being seen right through and found lacking. Kierkegaard wrote a lot about how people live looking over their shoulder at “the others,” afraid of being separate. In his treatise on despair he describes a person who, seeing how everyone else lives, finds it too risky to be himself and becomes a “copy,” worn smooth like a coin in circulation. From this angle, you might say that shame is often born from an outside gaze: we measure ourselves by the yardstick of other people's expectations. Kierkegaard proposed a different point of reference — to stand before yourself (and for him, before God) as a single, unrepeatable person. Before such a gaze you can't be a “not good enough copy,” because you aren't a copy.
shame.practice: Think about whose yardstick sounds in your shame. Is it your own voice, or the voice of some imaginary “everyone”?

guilt.text: Guilt is a heavy feeling, and Kierkegaard took it very seriously, without simplifying. He linked the capacity to feel guilt with freedom: only someone who could have acted otherwise can feel guilty. In The Concept of Anxiety he shows how closely anxiety and guilt are intertwined: anxiety precedes a free act, and guilt accompanies it. But Kierkegaard was also a thinker of forgiveness. In his religious works, forgiveness isn't forgetting but a new beginning. In Repetition he speaks of the possibility of receiving life anew without denying the past. From this angle, guilt isn't the end of the story but a place from which honest renewal can begin. You can acknowledge it without turning it into a verdict on yourself.
guilt.practice: Write down what you feel guilty about, and then one sentence about what your next step after this might look like, without denying what happened.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, and many people are ashamed of it. Kierkegaard offered an unexpected view: in his treatise on despair he wrote that envy is secret admiration. The one who envies is really admiring, but doesn't dare admit it to themselves and turns admiration into resentment. And in A Literary Review (1846) he described “leveling” — the mood of an age when envy becomes a way of trimming everyone down to one measure so that no one stands out. From this angle, your envy can be a signpost: it shows what truly fills you with admiration and what you'd like to develop in yourself. Rather than suppressing envy, you can “decode” it — and give it back its original meaning of admiration.
envy.practice: Rephrase your envy as admiration: “What I admire in this person is…”. What of this could you make your own?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are very heavy states, and it's important not to blame yourself for them. In his treatise on despair (1849), Kierkegaard describes despair not as a stormy drama but often as a quiet, unnoticed state: a person lives, works, socializes — but as if not present in their own life, not being themselves. He even noted that the most common despair is the kind that doesn't know it is despair. From this angle, the feeling of emptiness may not be empty at all: it's a signal that your self is asking for attention. For Kierkegaard, the way out of despair is to dare to “be yourself,” to establish an honest relationship with yourself. This doesn't happen in a moment; it's a path of small honest steps, and the first of them is noticing that you feel empty.
emptiness.practice: Ask yourself: at what moment in the past week was I closest to myself? What was I doing then?

confusion.text: Confusion arises when it's unclear where to go and who to be. Kierkegaard knew this state well: he himself agonized over choosing his path — in love, in his vocation. He believed that life can't be derived from a system like a theorem: no philosophy will make the decision for you. Hence his idea of the “leap”: you pass to a new way of life not through endless reasoning but through a decision that always carries risk. From this angle, confusion is a natural pause before a choice, not a sign of your inability. Kierkegaard also offers the comfort that the meaning of the road traveled often becomes visible only later. Right now you may not understand where you're going, and that's all right.
confusion.practice: What's the smallest step you could take, even without knowing where the whole road leads? Write it down.

quote.text: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are honest signals that your strength has become smaller than the demands on it. Kierkegaard wrote ironically about people so absorbed in their affairs that they have no time to be themselves. He considered bustle and “busyness” one of the ways of running away from yourself: as long as we're busy, we don't have to ask ourselves the main questions. From this angle, you might say that burnout happens when we live for a long time for the sake of external tasks, forgetting the inner. Kierkegaard reminded us that the self isn't a role or a function but a person's relationship to themselves. Rest, then, isn't idleness but a return to that relationship: to a silence in which your own voice can be heard again. You don't have to earn such rest.
fatigue.practice: Sit for two minutes in silence, without your phone or tasks. Notice: what sounds in you when outside demands fall quiet for a minute?

boredom.text: Boredom may seem trivial, but Kierkegaard devoted a whole essay to it — “Crop Rotation” in the first volume of Either/Or. His aesthete hero claims that boredom is the root of all evil and proposes a clever “rotation of crops”: not changing fields, but changing the way you look at the same thing, playing with impressions. But Kierkegaard shows that this is still a trap of the “aesthetic stage”: a life lived for what's interesting sooner or later exhausts itself. From this angle, boredom is a signal that the chase after impressions no longer nourishes you. The way out, for Kierkegaard, lies not in new stimuli but in the transition to the “ethical” stage: to choice, commitment, something you are responsible for. Boredom can be a door, not a dead end.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: what in my life could I take a small responsibility for — not because it's interesting, but because it matters? Write down one thing.

joy.text: Joy is a gift, and you can accept it without justifying it. Kierkegaard, known as a thinker of anxiety, also wrote beautiful pages about joy — in the discourses The Lily in the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849). He asks what we can learn from the lily and the bird, and one of his discourses answers: joy. In his view, joy means being truly in the present, “today,” not handing yourself over entirely to tomorrow's worries. The lily and the bird don't worry about tomorrow — that's why they are joyful. From this angle, joy doesn't need to be earned or saved up: it opens when you are here, wholly, in this moment. Kierkegaard believed such joy can be found even in the midst of difficulties.
joy.practice: Tell yourself: “Now — today.” Name three things in this moment that bring you joy, even just a little.

love.text: Love and tenderness are the most precious things in us, and Kierkegaard devoted a whole book to them — Works of Love (1847). He distinguished “preferential” love — for those especially dear to us — from love of the “neighbor,” directed at every person. One of his main ideas: love “builds up,” that is, it presupposes love in the other and thereby helps it grow. The one who loves sees more good in another than that person sees in themselves. From this angle, your tenderness isn't naivety but a creative force: it doesn't just reflect the world, it changes it. Kierkegaard also wrote that love is known by its fruits — by deeds, not only by feelings. Tenderness asks for small acts.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name one good quality you see in them — perhaps more clearly than they do themselves. How could you tell them about it?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and Kierkegaard saw something very deep in it. Several of his Upbuilding Discourses (1843) are devoted to a line from the Epistle of James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.” He reflects on how hard it can be to give thanks when life doesn't match our expectations, and on how gratitude changes the one who gives thanks. From this angle, gratitude isn't a polite formality but a way of relating to life: you stop only demanding from it and begin to receive. You needn't share Kierkegaard's religious views to take this thought from him: gratitude is an inner movement in which a person becomes gentler and freer.
gratitude.practice: Write down three gifts of this day that you didn't earn and didn't plan. What do you feel as you look at this list?

hope.text: Hope helps us go on living, and Kierkegaard valued it very highly. In his treatise on despair he wrote that what a person in despair needs above all is “possibility” — the sense that not everything is settled; without it, it's as if there were no air to breathe. For him this was connected with faith: “for God all things are possible.” In Works of Love he adds that love “hopes all things,” meaning that hope is also an attitude toward another person: not writing them off, leaving them a future. From this angle, hope isn't naive optimism but a decision to keep possibility open, even when you can't see it. You can apply this to yourself too: not passing a final verdict on yourself, leaving yourself a future.
hope.practice: Finish the sentence: “It's still possible that…” — about yourself or someone close to you. Let this possibility simply stay open.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender longing for the past, and you can live it gently. Kierkegaard thought a lot about memory. In Repetition (1843) he contrasted “recollection” and “repetition.” Recollection faces backward: it preserves what is lost, and so it is tinged with sadness. Repetition faces forward: it is the capacity to receive what is precious again — not copying the past, but living its meaning anew. And in Either/Or there's an essay on “the unhappiest one” — a person who lives only in recollection or only in expectation and is never present in the present. From this angle, nostalgia is beautiful as long as it doesn't take your “today” away from you. You can ask yourself: what of what I long for could be not brought back, but received anew?
nostalgia.practice: Choose one memory you miss. What was the heart of it — and how could that heart appear in your life now, in a new form?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it right now,” and its strength doesn't make you a bad person. Kierkegaard described a similar life under the name of the “aesthetic stage” — a life ruled by immediate desires and moods. His aesthete hero in the first volume of Either/Or admits himself that pleasure disappoints, while possibility does not. From this angle, you might say that a craving promises not so much a substance or a thing as the feeling that everything is about to be different. Kierkegaard saw the way out not in prohibition but in choice: in a person one day choosing themselves — not their desire, but the self who is experiencing that desire. A craving says “now or never.” But between the wave and the act there is always a moment, and in it, you live.
craving.practice: When a craving washes over you, tell yourself: “I notice the desire, and I am the one who notices it.” Wait for three slow breaths and note whether anything has changed.

addiction.text: Addiction is a long-standing circle that's hard to leave, and it isn't a moral failure. Kierkegaard would say that it touches the deepest part of a person — their self. In his treatise on despair he defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself. From this angle, you might say that in addiction this relation seems to pass over to something else: life becomes organized around a substance or a habit, and the person themselves is pushed aside. Kierkegaard also wrote about “purity of heart” — being able to will one thing rather than being torn apart. But he never thought a person manages this alone or all at once. For him, the path to oneself always passed through honesty, through a willingness to admit one's need and accept help.
addiction.practice: Finish the sentence: “If my life were built around me myself, it would have…”. If you feel like it, you can talk about this with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after a heavy evening: your body aches, and on top of that come anxiety, shame and gaps in memory. It's agonizing, and you don't need to finish yourself off. Kierkegaard clearly distinguished two ways of relating to your past. You can judge yourself endlessly — and then, in his view, a person despairs not only over the act but over themselves, and the despair becomes double. Or you can do what Judge William in the second volume of Either/Or calls “choosing yourself”: acknowledging your history as your own, neither disowning it nor drowning in it. From this angle, you might say that morning shame is a signal that you care. You don't need to settle everything today. It's enough to say to yourself honestly: “This happened to me, and I am here.”
hangover.practice: Take care of your body: water, fresh air. Then say aloud: “Yesterday happened to me. Today I can take one kind step,” — and name that step.

euphoria.text: A flash of euphoria is a vivid feeling when everything seems possible, and you can be glad of it. Kierkegaard understood this light well: his aesthete in Either/Or confesses that he would wish for himself not wealth or power but the passion for the possible — an eye that sees possibility everywhere. For Kierkegaard, “possibility” isn't an empty dream but one of the two sides of the self: a person is woven from the possible and the necessary, from flight and ground. From this angle, you might say that euphoria is a moment when the side of the possible suddenly shines at full strength. There's no need to put it out. Kierkegaard would suggest just one thing: so that the flash doesn't fly away entirely, tie it to something small and real. Then possibility becomes not only a feeling but part of your life.
euphoria.practice: Write down one possibility you see clearly right now, and one very small action with which you could touch it this week.

crash.text: A sharp comedown after a high can be very hard — as if the party were over and you'd been left alone in an empty hall. Kierkegaard wrote a whole book about this — Repetition (1843). Its narrator, Constantin Constantius, once had a wonderful time in Berlin and decided to go back to repeat it all. But nothing worked: the room wasn't right, the theater gave no pleasure, everything seemed faded. From this angle, you might say that a slump is often born from trying to hold on to or repeat the high. Kierkegaard distinguished this kind of repetition from the real one: when life isn't brought back by force but received anew, as a gift — in a new form. Right now you don't need to bring anything back. You can simply let yourself come down and wait for what comes.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “I don't need to repeat yesterday's high.” Notice one small good thing in today that is nothing like that high.

panic.text: Panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. It's genuinely hard. In The Concept of Anxiety Kierkegaard offered an image that helps many people: someone who looks down into a yawning abyss grows dizzy, and the cause, he wrote, lies not only in the abyss but also in the eye that looks into it. From this angle, you might say that panic, too, pulls your gaze into the abyss — toward the worst thing that could happen. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. And when you're dizzy, something simple helps: shifting your gaze to what is near and solid, and holding on to what you can touch.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor, lay your palm on a solid surface and breathe out for longer than you breathe in. Name five objects around you that are close by.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is all this for,” thoughts of finitude and the abyss — is one of the heaviest experiences. Kierkegaard knew it from the inside. At twenty-two he wrote in his journal that he needed to find a truth that was true for him, an idea for which he wanted to live. Not a general system, but his own meaning. And in the discourse “At a Graveside” (1845) he wrote that the thought of finitude can teach “earnestness”: it makes today precious and keeps you from putting off what matters most. From this angle, you might say that your dread isn't a sign that there's no meaning, but the beginning of your own question about meaning. Such a question isn't answered in one night. You carry it within you, and little by little it begins to change how you live today.
dread.practice: Finish the sentence: “What truly matters to me today is…”. Let the answer be quite small and concrete.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you're not where you should be is very draining. Kierkegaard described it with astonishing precision. In the first volume of Either/Or there's an “ecstatic lecture”: marry, and you'll regret it; don't marry, and you'll regret that too; do it, and you'll regret it; don't, and you'll regret it. And in the essay on “the unhappiest one” he paints a person who is never present in their own life: they live now in hope of the future, now in memory of the past. From this angle, you might say that the fear of missing out is a life lived “outside yourself,” in other people's places and possibilities. Kierkegaard's answer is choice: Judge William says that what matters is not so much the right option as the act of choosing itself, in which a person becomes themselves. Where you are is where your life begins.
fomo.practice: Tell yourself: “I choose to be here.” Name one thing that exists only in your today — and stay with it for a minute.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts can be especially hard: everything seems huge and unsolvable. You're not alone in this. In Christian Discourses (1848), Kierkegaard devoted a separate reflection to worry about tomorrow and called it “the worry of self-torment.” He wrote that the bird of the air doesn't know this worry, because it has no “tomorrow” — only “today.” From this angle, you might say that night thoughts are almost always about tomorrow: about what hasn't happened yet and what nothing can be done about right now. Kierkegaard would suggest not fighting these thoughts but gently bringing yourself back to “today” — to this room, this breath, this moment, in which there are no tomorrow's tasks.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself: “Tomorrow's things are for tomorrow.” Put your palm on your chest and count ten slow out-breaths.

betrayal.text: Betrayal is a deep wound: what collapses is not only a relationship but your faith in your own trust. Your pain is justified. In Works of Love (1847), Kierkegaard reflected on what to do with trust after being deceived. He noted that mistrust can be a self-deception too: it seems wise, but in fact it simply chooses the worst explanation. And he voiced a bold thought: whoever deceives the one who loves ultimately deceives themselves most of all, depriving themselves of what is most precious. From this angle, you might say that your trust wasn't foolishness — it was your capacity to love, and it still belongs to you. You don't have to forgive anyone on a schedule. But you can refuse to let this wound take you away from yourself.
betrayal.practice: Write: “My trust says about me that I…”. Add one quality you want to keep despite what happened.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a burning feeling, and there's no shame in feeling it: it shows how much another person means to you. In Works of Love, Kierkegaard distinguished “preferential” love — for those especially dear to us — from love of the “neighbor.” He wrote of the first with great respect, but honestly noted its vulnerability: immediate love can change within itself and turn into jealousy. From this angle, you might say that jealousy is love seized by the fear of loss. Kierkegaard didn't demand giving it up, but suggested adding a second dimension to love: seeing the beloved not only as “my” person but also as a separate, free individual. This doesn't extinguish the feeling, but it gives it more air.
jealousy.practice: Name one quality of the person you love that belongs only to them — not to you and not to your relationship. What do you feel as you think about it?

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is a heavy load, and behind it there is almost always a real injustice. In his treatise on despair, Kierkegaard described a striking state: a person has grown so attached to their pain that they can no longer give it up, because it has become part of them, proof that they were right. From this angle, you might say that resentment sometimes holds on to us not because we want to suffer, but because parting with it feels like a betrayal of ourselves. Kierkegaard didn't demand hasty forgiveness. He suggested seeing that the self is larger than any wound: it can acknowledge the wound — and still not live only for it. Letting go begins not with forgetting but with a question: who would I be without this weight?
resentment.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I loosened my grip on this resentment a little, I'm afraid that…”. Just look at the answer, without deciding anything.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and no one has the right to hurry it. Kierkegaard lived through it himself: in 1841 he broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen and, according to his own journals, kept thinking about her all his life. This wound runs through many of his books. In Repetition, a young man going through a love drama writes long letters and suffers, not knowing how to go on living. Kierkegaard shows that it is possible to get through such pain — not by trying to bring back the past, but through life being given back little by little, in a new form. From this angle, you might say that your grief isn't an end but part of your self's becoming. For now, it's enough simply to allow yourself to grieve.
heartbreak.practice: Write a short letter you won't send: what you'd like to say to this love in farewell. Then simply put it aside.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're about to be exposed is very common, and it visits conscientious people especially often. Kierkegaard knew the game of masks well: he wrote many books under pseudonyms and pondered where the real author was behind them. But above all, he criticized “the public,” the faceless crowd whose judgments we submit to, although it is, in his words, an abstraction, a phantom. What mattered most to him was “the single individual” — a person who stands before life (for Kierkegaard, before God) on their own, not before an audience. From this angle, you might say that the impostor is a role we play for imaginary spectators. Before yourself you aren't an “impostor” but a person on the way, learning and growing.
impostor.practice: Imagine the auditorium is empty. What can you really do, and love doing, when no one is judging? Write down one thing.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and a harsh inner critic cause enormous pain, and you don't deserve that verdict. In his treatise on despair, Kierkegaard described a form of suffering in which a person despairingly does not want to be themselves and would like to be rid of themselves. He saw in this not a vice but a sickness of the self, which calls for gentleness, not fresh reproaches. And in Works of Love he has a striking thought: the commandment “love your neighbor as yourself” presupposes that the right love of oneself and love of one's neighbor are, at heart, one and the same. From this angle, you might say that the inner critic violates not only your peace but the very nature of love. Loving yourself in the right way isn't selfishness but part of knowing how to love.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine someone you sincerely love. Say one sentence to yourself in the same tone you would use with them.

helplessness.text: Helplessness, the feeling that you can't change anything, is a very heavy state, and it's not your fault. Kierkegaard devoted an unexpected reflection to it — the upbuilding discourse “To Need God Is a Human Being's Highest Perfection” (1844). He wrote that admitting you can do little on your own isn't a defeat but the beginning of a genuine relationship to life. For Kierkegaard this was a religious path. But even outside faith, his thought can be read this way: powerlessness lays bare the fact that human beings aren't made to cope alone. From this angle, you might say that what matters now is not pretending you're all-powerful, but allowing yourself to need others — help, support, someone else's presence beside you.
helplessness.practice: Name one person you could ask for at least a little support. Write down what exactly you could ask them for.

procrastination.text: The state of “I can't get started” is exhausting, and it doesn't mean you're lazy. Kierkegaard described it in the “Diapsalmata” — the aesthete's aphorisms in the first volume of Either/Or. The aesthete complains: riding is too violent, walking too tiring; lie down — and then you'll have to either stay lying down or get up again, and he wants neither. He doesn't feel like anything. From this angle, you might say that procrastination is life among endless possibilities, none of which has been chosen. Kierkegaard believed that no amount of preparation cancels the “leap”: a decision that can't be calculated in advance can only be made. The leap doesn't have to be huge. Sometimes it's simply the first movement of your hand toward the task.
procrastination.practice: Choose the tiniest first step, one that will take two minutes. Say out loud: “I'm starting” — and do only that.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — a move, emigration — is a hard experience, as if the ground were slipping from under your feet. Kierkegaard lived almost his whole life in Copenhagen, but in his most difficult period — after breaking off his engagement — he went to Berlin, and there he wrote most of Either/Or. Far from home, he was looking not for a new place but for himself. For Kierkegaard, the self isn't a place or a setting but a person's relationship to themselves, which they can build anew anywhere. From this angle, you might say that moving takes away outer supports but leaves the main one — your capacity to become yourself. Homesickness is legitimate. But in a new place, too, there's something no one can take from you: your own path.
uprooted.practice: Write: “Wherever I am, I remain someone who…”. Add one thing that stays yours in any city.

overload.text: Overload, the endless feed, informational noise — all this really is tiring. Kierkegaard, surprisingly, described it almost two hundred years ago. In A Literary Review (1846) he speaks of “the present age” as an age of reflection and chatter: everyone discusses everything, the press creates “the public,” and the individual dissolves into an endless exchange of opinions and puts off living their own life. From this angle, you might say that overload isn't only fatigue from information but also the loss of your own voice. Kierkegaard knew a simple remedy: he walked around Copenhagen almost every day and considered walks the source of his best thoughts. Sometimes the only answer to noise is to step out of it, even briefly.
overload.practice: If you can, go outside for five minutes without your phone. If not, close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you without naming them.

quote.text: I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

unreality.text: The feeling that nothing is quite real can be very frightening, and it's hard to tell others about. Kierkegaard described similar states. In his dissertation On the Concept of Irony (1841) he portrayed a person for whom all of actuality has “lost its validity” — everything has become distant, as if on a stage. And in his treatise on despair he wrote of the “despair of infinitude,” when the self seems to evaporate into fantasy and loses touch with the concrete. From this angle, you might say that the feeling of unreality isn't your fault and isn't emptiness, but a sign that your connection to the concrete has weakened for a while. Kierkegaard saw the way back in simple things: in small, everyday actions that return a person to the “here.”
unreality.practice: Do one concrete thing with your hands: wash a cup, stroke a piece of fabric. Notice the sensations — temperature, texture — and name them to yourself.

awe.text: Trembling before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. Kierkegaard knew it. In the discourses The Lily in the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849) he wrote that the first thing the lily and the bird teach is silence. Before the grandeur of the world, a person usually tries to say something, explain it, remember it. But the lily and the bird simply are — and there is more reverence in their silence than in all our words. For Kierkegaard, such silence was a relationship to God; but his thought can be read more broadly too: awe is a moment when words are superfluous. From this angle, you might say that the best way to live through awe is not to hurry to describe it, photograph it or share it, but simply to be in it.
awe.practice: Spend a minute in silence before whatever filled you with awe. Don't describe it, even to yourself — just look.

relief.text: Relief is a quiet warmth after long tension, and it's worth savoring. Kierkegaard described it in Repetition (1843). The young man in this book suffers for a long time in an unresolvable situation, and when it unexpectedly resolves, he writes a simple sentence: he has become himself again. For Kierkegaard this was true “repetition” — not the return of the past, but receiving yourself anew, as a gift. From this angle, you might say that relief isn't just the disappearance of a weight but a moment when you come back to yourself again. You don't need to rush to fill the freed-up space. Let yourself feel what it's like to be yourself again.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and say to yourself: “I am myself again.” Notice where in your body this resonates.

calm.text: Calm and peace are a precious state in which it's good simply to be. Kierkegaard drew a picture of such calm in Fear and Trembling (1843). His “knight of faith” looks nothing like a hero: he looks like an ordinary tax collector, walks the streets, looks forward to his dinner, strolls in the woods and delights in everything he sees. Outwardly there's nothing special about him, but he is fully present in the finite, in ordinary life. For Kierkegaard this calm was the fruit of faith; but his image can be read more broadly too. From this angle, you might say that real calm isn't an escape from the world but the ability to be wholly present in the simplest day. Right now, perhaps, this is exactly what you're feeling.
calm.practice: Notice one completely ordinary thing around you — the taste of tea, light on the wall — and stay with it for a minute, as with something precious.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a lively, joyful state, and it's worth receiving with gratitude. Kierkegaard wrote with astonishing force: in a few years he produced dozens of books. He valued “passion” — not a storm of emotions but a fullness of inner engagement without which, in his view, one can't truly exist. In the Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846), his pseudonym Johannes Climacus says that for a living person truth isn't an abstraction but the way they live in it. From this angle, you might say that inspiration is a moment when thought and life come together. Kierkegaard wouldn't urge you to analyze it. What would matter to him is that it not remain just a mood, but take shape, at least a little, in action.
inspiration.practice: Write down right now what has come to you, without editing. Then note one small action with which you could put it into practice in the next few days.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude flares up suddenly and leaves an unpleasant aftertaste: am I really like this? Kierkegaard helps you look at this feeling without self-flagellation. In The Sickness unto Death he wrote that the measure of the self is always that before which it places itself. If we measure ourselves by other people, our sense of self rises and falls with their successes and failures. From this angle, schadenfreude isn't so much malice as a symptom that you've temporarily started living in someone else's coordinate system: another's fall feels like your rise. Kierkegaard wouldn't shame you. He would ask: before what do I want to be myself? When the measure is your own life and its task, someone else's failure stops meaning anything for your self.
schadenfreude.practice: Finish the sentence: “Their failure made me feel, for a second…”. Then ask: by what yardstick am I measuring myself right now?

contempt.text: Contempt is often born of real disappointment in a person, and it can be understandable. In his dissertation On the Concept of Irony, Kierkegaard wrote about a stance of superiority from which you can look down on everything. He acknowledged its power, but noted that if you make it your permanent point of view, it isolates you — you end up above everyone, and therefore alone. In Works of Love he offered the opposite view: the one who loves “presupposes” the possibility of good in another, even if it can't be seen right now. Contempt, by contrast, sees a person as finished, defined once and for all by their worst act. From this angle, you don't have to give up your judgment, but you can leave a crack in it for possibility: a person is not only what they have done. And you, too, don't have to live on a cold height.
contempt.practice: Finish the sentence: “This person did…, but they are not only that. Perhaps there is also…in them”. Even one word in the second part counts.

disgust.text: Disgust — at a situation, at people or at yourself — is a heavy, repelling feeling. Kierkegaard paid especially close attention to its inward-turned form. In The Sickness unto Death he distinguished despair over something external from despair over oneself, when a person looks at their own weakness with disgust. Unexpectedly, he considered the second a deeper state, and one closer to healing: in it a person at least sees themselves and takes themselves seriously. From this angle, disgust with yourself isn't proof of your worthlessness but a sign that you care who you are. Kierkegaard didn't agree with the inner verdict. He suggested taking the next step: accepting this weak self as your own — the only material from which you can go on becoming yourself.
disgust.practice: Finish the sentence: “What I find disgusting in myself shows that what matters to me is…”. Look at the second half as a signpost, not a verdict.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were wronged, and something inside demands that justice be restored. In Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing, Kierkegaard described “double-mindedness” — a state in which a person is torn between different aims and stops being whole. From this angle, you might say that revenge quietly shifts the center of your life: more and more of your thoughts and strength start to revolve around the person who hurt you, and they, without even meaning to, gain power over you. Kierkegaard didn't demand hasty forgiveness and didn't deny that you were in the right. But he would ask: do I want my self to be defined by this person? You can acknowledge your anger fully — and still put your own life back at the center, your own task, your own “one thing,” not someone else's act.
revenge.practice: Estimate how much of your thinking today this person took up. Choose one activity that will give you back a little of your own time.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you is especially hard, because shame follows it: how can you be angry with someone you love? In Works of Love, Kierkegaard devoted a chapter to the duty of loving the people we see. His thought is that we easily love an imagined image — the ideal partner, parent, child — while the real person beside us inevitably fails to match it. From this angle, anger often flares where image and reality meet: “they should have been different.” This doesn't mean there's no love — on the contrary, it means your expectations are great. Kierkegaard suggested not giving up love but transferring it from the image to the person as they are. There's no need to shame your anger; you can ask it which image it has just collided with.
anger_at_loved.practice: Describe how you expected your loved one to be in this situation, and how they actually were. What would it mean to love the second one?

ambivalence.text: Loving a person and at the same time not being able to stand them is a state you want to escape quickly by choosing one feeling. Kierkegaard knew it from the inside: he loved Regine Olsen, broke off their engagement, and wrote about it all his life, never reducing his feelings to one. His philosophy explains why this isn't a malfunction. In The Sickness unto Death, the self is described as a synthesis of opposites — the finite and the infinite, freedom and necessity — and as a relation that relates itself to itself. From this angle, mixed feelings are the natural state of a being woven from contradictions. The task isn't for one feeling to win, but how you yourself relate to both. You can hold them together without rushing to a final decision.
ambivalence.practice: Write: “I love… and I can't bear…” — in one sentence, joined by “and,” not “but.” Notice what it's like to hold them together.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure or even the death of a gravely ill loved one often frightens us: was there not enough love? Kierkegaard helps us see that relief and love live on different levels. Relief is a response to the end of tension, fear and exhausting caregiving. Love, for Kierkegaard, doesn't end along with circumstances. In Works of Love there's a chapter on the love that remembers one who has died; he called it the most unselfish and the most faithful love, since it receives nothing in return. From this angle, relief doesn't cancel love: you can breathe out and go on loving, remembering, being grateful. Kierkegaard wouldn't judge you. He would more likely say that your capacity to grieve over your relief itself speaks of the depth of your attachment.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down one memory of the person or the relationship that is dear to you. Let it exist alongside the relief, without arguing with it.

indifference.text: When something should move you and doesn't, it's easy to get frightened for yourself. In A Literary Review, Kierkegaard described his age as sensible and passionless: people discuss a lot, know a little about everything, but are rarely truly gripped by anything. He saw this not as a personal vice but as a sickness of the age, where a stream of information replaces living engagement. From this angle, you might say that your indifference isn't necessarily callousness. It may be weariness from having to have an opinion and a feeling about everything at once. Kierkegaard valued “inwardness” — what can't be put on show and can't be summoned on command. So there's no point faking a feeling that isn't there. Better to honestly leave room: living engagement comes when a thing becomes yours, not everyone's.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: is there anything in this situation that concerns me personally, not “everyone”? If you find even one detail, stay with it.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — is understandable when life has grown too tight. Kierkegaard described it ironically in the essay “Crop Rotation” in Either/Or. His aesthete hero lists: one person gets tired of living in the country and goes to the city; tired of his homeland, he goes abroad; tired of Europe, he goes to America. Kierkegaard shows that such a change of circumstances often just carries the boredom to a new place. But in the same book Judge William, the voice of the ethical life, proposes another path — “choosing yourself,” that is, taking on your life and its task. From this angle, you can ask: do I want to escape the place, or the way I live in it? Sometimes a change of circumstances is right; sometimes it's choosing yourself within them.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I left, I would finally become…”. Does this new “me” have one small step that's possible right here?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be embarrassing and unsettling. Kierkegaard wrote a lot about a life drawn toward the possible — in Either/Or this is the world of the aesthete, for whom what's most alluring is not what is but what could be. In The Sickness unto Death he described a self that drifts off into imagined possibilities and loses touch with reality, and a self that clings only to necessity and suffocates. From this angle, the unavailable attracts partly because it is pure possibility — something untested by reality. Kierkegaard wouldn't pass a verdict on you. He'd suggest an honest question: what in this desire is about the particular person, and what is about what you yourself are missing in your own life?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “what draws me to this person” and “what's missing in my life.” Just look at whether there's a connection between them.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is familiar to many, and it turns a simple meeting into something like an exam. Kierkegaard offered an unusual image in Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. We're used to thinking that we stand on a stage and the people around us are the audience. He turns this picture around: each person is the actor, and there is only one true spectator — the one before whom a person answers for their life. For Kierkegaard this is God; but even in a secular reading the meaning remains: the main question isn't “how do I look in the eyes of the crowd?” but “was I myself just now?” From this angle, nervousness doesn't make you worse, and the judgment of every passing glance stops being final. The spectator who really matters looks not at your polish but at your honesty.
social_anxiety.practice: After a nerve-racking meeting, ask yourself not “how did I come across?” but “where was I myself today?” Write down at least one moment.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is tiring: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In his discourses on the lilies of the field and the birds of the air, Kierkegaard made a subtle observation. The bird doesn't worry about tomorrow — not because it's wiser, but because it has no tomorrow. A human being, though, can imagine tomorrow — and this is both our greatness and the source of our worries. From this angle, your anxiety about the unknown is the flip side of a very human ability to see ahead. Kierkegaard didn't suggest giving it up. He suggested learning one thing from the bird: to live today so fully that tomorrow doesn't take it away entirely. The future remains unknown, but you still have “today” — the only time in which you can act.
uncertainty.practice: Write down one thing that belongs only to today and that you can do. Do it, without settling tomorrow.

waiting.text: Waiting for an answer, results or news stretches time out, and it's hard to find your place in it. Kierkegaard wrote one of his early upbuilding discourses on “To Gain One's Soul in Patience.” His thought is unexpected: patience doesn't just help you get through the waiting — in it, a person gains themselves. When we can't speed anything up, all that remains is how we relate to the waiting, and it's precisely here that the self becomes visible. From this angle, the time of waiting isn't an empty gap but time that also belongs to your life. Kierkegaard didn't demand serenity. The nervousness will stay, but you can ask yourself: who do I want to be while I wait? This question gives back to you some of what waiting seems to take away.
waiting.practice: Finish the sentence: “While I wait, I want to be…”. Choose one small action that fits that word.

regret.text: Regret can be very persistent — about what you did and what you didn't. In Either/Or, through the mouth of his aesthete hero, Kierkegaard ironically showed that regret lies in wait whatever you choose: marry, and you'll regret it; don't marry, and you'll regret that too. It sounds bleak, but it lifts part of the burden: there never was a path free of regret. And in the second part of the book, Judge William proposes a different answer — to choose yourself wholly, including your past. For Kierkegaard, a person who accepts their history neither erases it nor punishes themselves for it, but acknowledges: this is me too, and I go on with it. From this angle, regret isn't a verdict but part of the material from which you keep becoming yourself.
regret.practice: Write one sentence about what you regret, beginning with the words: “This, too, is part of my story, and from it I know that…”.

quote.text: Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, and you will also regret it; marry or do not marry, you will regret it either way.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

longing.text: Longing for a particular person pulls you back toward what was. In Repetition, Kierkegaard distinguished two ways of being connected with what has been lost: recollection and repetition. Recollection looks back and keeps the past as it was; repetition is the same movement, but forward: what was dear can become alive again in the present, even if in a new form. In Either/Or he described “the unhappiest one” — a person who lives only in recollection and is therefore absent from their own life. From this angle, you don't need to drive your longing away: it speaks of love. But you can ask what of what this person gave you can live in you now too — in a habit, a word, a way of seeing the world.
longing.practice: Name one thing you took on from this person or lived through with them. Do something in its spirit today.

quote.text: Repetition and recollection are the same movement, except in opposite directions.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — heavy news, war, injustice — can grow to a size you can't live with. Kierkegaard almost always thought about the single individual, and this helps here in an unexpected way. In Works of Love he insisted that love is directed not at humanity in general but at the “neighbor” — the concrete person next to you. From this angle, you might say: pain for the whole world at once is almost unbearable, because “the world” is an abstraction, and you are a concrete person. Compassion doesn't have to embrace everything. It becomes real when it finds one face, one task, one act. Your sensitivity isn't a mistake. But you can carry it on a human scale — the scale of the neighbor, not the whole planet.
world_pain.practice: Name one specific person — near you or far away — whom you can help today, write to, or simply give some attention.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts, and the pain isn't exaggerated. In The Sickness unto Death, Kierkegaard gives the example of a girl who has lost her beloved. He notes that she despairs not only over him but over herself — over the self she wanted to gain in his love, which now seems unbearable to her. From this angle, rejection wounds so deeply because we invest our self in someone else's choice. Kierkegaard didn't deny this pain. But his answer is that the self can't be grounded in another person's decision: it is rooted deeper — in your own relationship to yourself. A refusal takes away the hope of a particular future, but it can't take you away from yourself.
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: “With this person, I hoped to become…”. Ask yourself: which of this can I become without them?

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be an almost constant background. In The Concept of Anxiety, Kierkegaard wrote that anxiety, unlike fear, is directed not at a concrete threat but at possibility — at what could happen. That's why it's so hard to calm with arguments: everything is fine right now, but the possibility of loss remains. Kierkegaard, unexpectedly, saw anxiety as a teacher. He believed that anxiety, if you don't run from it, teaches us our freedom and our bond with what is dear to us. From this angle, your fear isn't a weakness but a sign of how much the people close to you mean to you. There's no need to be ashamed of it. You can learn to live with it: notice it, name it, and not let it alone decide what is true.
abandonment.practice: When the fear rises, name it out loud: “This is fear of a possibility, not a fact.” Then name one thing that is really here right now.

quote.text: Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the ultimate.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
quote.source: The Concept of Anxiety, ch. V (1844)

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is one of the loneliest pains. In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard told a parable about a young man in love with a princess who is beyond his reach. The young man doesn't renounce his love or try to forget it by pretending it was foolishness. He makes what Kierkegaard called “infinite resignation”: he gives up the claim to its fulfillment but keeps the love itself as part of his life. Kierkegaard writes that such love remains eternally young in him. From this angle, you might say: your love wasn't a mistake, and it doesn't have to disappear for you to go on living. You can let go of expecting an answer without betraying what you felt. It's a hard movement, and it takes time.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love revealed to you in yourself. Try telling yourself: “I can keep this without expecting an answer.”

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply, and Kierkegaard knew this from his own experience. In 1846 the satirical paper The Corsair began mocking him: it drew caricatures, ridiculed his gait and even his uneven trouser legs. On the streets of Copenhagen, boys laughed at him. Kierkegaard took it hard, but it was precisely then that he formulated especially clearly the idea of “the single individual” — the separate person who doesn't dissolve into the crowd's judgment. As he understood it, the laughter of the public can't determine who a person really is. From this angle, your pain is real, but humiliation is what others did to you, not what you have become. The dignity of the self lies deeper than anyone's mockery can reach.
humiliation.practice: Finish the sentence: “What was done to me was…. But I am…”. In the second part, name at least one thing that has remained untouched.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can stay with a person for years. In The Concept of Anxiety Kierkegaard wrote that a human being is a synthesis of soul and body, united by spirit — that is, by a living relationship to oneself. The body here isn't an appendage or a mistake but part of who you are. In The Sickness unto Death he described a despair in which a person doesn't want to be themselves and dreams of becoming someone else, as if changing clothes. From this angle, shame about your body can be one form of this unwillingness — a refusal of your “necessity,” of what is given and not chosen. Kierkegaard saw the way out not in loving everything at once, but in consenting to be yourself, this person, in this body — and moving on from there.
body_shame.practice: Tell yourself silently: “This is my body, and I am it too.” Don't evaluate; just notice what happens when you say it.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, the world narrows, and this can be enraging, frightening and exhausting. Kierkegaard was in fragile health all his life, and in his journals he wrote of his “thorn in the flesh” — the apostle Paul's phrase for a suffering that doesn't go away. He devoted one of his upbuilding discourses to this image. Kierkegaard didn't pretend that such a thorn was good or useful. But his philosophy suggests that the self isn't only a body but a relation that relates itself to itself. Illness limits you, but the way you relate to it, and to yourself within it, remains yours. From this angle, you don't have to demand heroism of yourself or pretend to be well. It's enough to remain yourself within what is possible today.
illness.practice: Finish the sentence: “Even now, despite the illness, I remain a person who…”. Name one trait the illness hasn't taken away.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a joyful, well-earned feeling. Kierkegaard invited us to see in it what makes it truly healthy. For him, a person's main task was to become themselves — that is, not simply to get a result, but to choose and carry out something as their own act. Judge William in Either/Or describes the ethical life as a life in which a person answers for what they do. From this angle, the best pride isn't superiority over others but joy that you really acted and became a little more yourself. Such pride doesn't need comparing and doesn't need hiding. You can simply live it as a moment when the self coincides with its deed.
pride.practice: Write down what choice you made on the way to this result. What does that choice say about who you are?

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet state in which sorrow feels almost like kin. Kierkegaard knew it as few others did: all his life he called himself a melancholic, and in the “Diapsalmata” of Either/Or his aesthete speaks of his sorrow as a secure refuge. Kierkegaard saw in melancholy depth and sensitivity, an ability to hear what gets lost in the bustle. But in the second part of the same book, Judge William gently objects: melancholy can become a place where a person hides from choice. Both voices are valuable. From this angle, you can let yourself stay in this sadness without hurrying to chase it away — and notice whether it's calling you toward something. Melancholy can be both a home and a door.
melancholy.practice: Ask your melancholy: “What are you about?” — and write down the first thing that comes. The answer can be a single word.

quote.text: My grief is my baronial castle.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
